claim: COPII mediates formation of membrane vesicles that export newly synthesised proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Coat protein complex II (COPII) mediates formation of the membrane vesicles that export newly synthesised proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: This is a well-established function of COPII stated in the abstract, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The inner COPII proteins bind to cargo and membrane, linking them to the outer COPII components.
source: The inner COPII proteins bind to cargo and membrane, linking them to the outer COPII components that form a cage around the vesicle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COPII function stated in the abstract.

claim: The outer COPII components form a cage around the vesicle.
source: The inner COPII proteins bind to cargo and membrane, linking them to the outer COPII components that form a cage around the vesicle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COPII structure stated in the abstract.

claim: Regulated flexibility in coat architecture is essential for transport of a variety of differently sized cargoes.
source: Regulated flexibility in coat architecture is essential for transport of a variety of differently sized cargoes, but structural data on the assembled coat has not been available.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about COPII function requirements.

claim: Structural data on the assembled COPII coat has not been available prior to this study.
source: Regulated flexibility in coat architecture is essential for transport of a variety of differently sized cargoes, but structural data on the assembled coat has not been available.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the study, representing a gap in existing knowledge.

claim: The authors used cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging to determine the structure of the complete, membrane-assembled COPII coat.
source: We have used cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging to determine the structure of the complete, membrane-assembled COPII coat.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The study describes a novel arrangement of the outer coat.
source: We describe a novel arrangement of the outer coat and find that the inner coat can assemble into regular lattices.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on structural data.

claim: The inner coat can assemble into regular lattices.
source: We describe a novel arrangement of the outer coat and find that the inner coat can assemble into regular lattices.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on structural data.

claim: The data reveal how coat subunits interact with one another and with the membrane.
source: The data reveal how coat subunits interact with one another and with the membrane, suggesting how coordinated assembly of inner and outer coats can mediate and regulate packaging of vesicles ranging from small spheres to large tubular carriers.
evidence: This describes findings from the structural data obtained in the study.

claim: Coordinated assembly of inner and outer coats can mediate and regulate packaging of vesicles ranging from small spheres to large tubular carriers.
source: The data reveal how coat subunits interact with one another and with the membrane, suggesting how coordinated assembly of inner and outer coats can mediate and regulate packaging of vesicles ranging from small spheres to large tubular carriers.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural data, representing an inference from the findings.

claim: Sar1 exposes an N-terminal amphipathic helix upon exchange of GDP for GTP that inserts into the outer ER membrane leaflet, promoting curvature.
source: Upon exchange of GDP for GTP (catalysed by Sec12), Sar1 exposes an N-terminal amphipathic helix that inserts into the outer ER membrane leaflet, promoting curvature (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2005.

claim: Sec12 catalyses the exchange of GDP for GTP on Sar1.
source: Upon exchange of GDP for GTP (catalysed by Sec12), Sar1 exposes an N-terminal amphipathic helix that inserts into the outer ER membrane leaflet, promoting curvature (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2005.

claim: Sar1 recruits heterodimers of Sec23 and Sec24 to the membrane, forming the inner layer of the COPII coat.
source: Sar1 recruits heterodimers of Sec23 and Sec24 to the membrane, thereby forming the inner layer of the COPII coat (Matsuoka et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matsuoka et al., 1998.

claim: Sec24 binds transport cargo.
source: Sec23/24 is an adaptor complex: Sec24 binds transport cargo while Sec23 interacts with Sar1 and recruits Sec13/31 (Miller et al., 2002; Bi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2002 and Bi et al., 2007.

claim: Sec23 interacts with Sar1 and recruits Sec13/31.
source: Sec23/24 is an adaptor complex: Sec24 binds transport cargo while Sec23 interacts with Sar1 and recruits Sec13/31 (Miller et al., 2002; Bi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2002 and Bi et al., 2007.

claim: Sec13/31 heterotetramers constitute the outer coat layer.
source: Sec13/31 heterotetramers constitute the outer coat layer, thought to polymerise into cages that enclose the budding membrane (Fath et al., 2007; Stagg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fath et al., 2007 and Stagg et al., 2008.

claim: Sec13/31 is thought to polymerise into cages that enclose the budding membrane.
source: Sec13/31 heterotetramers constitute the outer coat layer, thought to polymerise into cages that enclose the budding membrane (Fath et al., 2007; Stagg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fath et al., 2007 and Stagg et al., 2008, and represents a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: GTP hydrolysis on Sar1, activated by Sec23 and further accelerated by Sec31, promotes fission of the bud and coat depolymerization.
source: GTP hydrolysis on Sar1, activated by Sec23 and further accelerated by Sec31, completes the cycle by promoting fission of the bud and coat depolymerization (Zanetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zanetti et al., 2012.

claim: X-ray crystallography has been used to obtain structural models for all the COPII coat subunits.
source: X-ray crystallography has been used to obtain structural models for all the coat subunits (Bi et al., 2002; Fath et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bi et al., 2002 and Fath et al., 2007.

claim: Available structural data for the inner coat is limited to isolated subcomplexes.
source: Available structural data for the inner coat is limited to isolated subcomplexes.
evidence: This represents a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy has been used to derive models of Sec13/31 cages formed in vitro under high salt conditions in the absence of membrane.
source: Progress has been made in understanding how the outer coat subunits assemble into a coat by using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy to derive models of Sec13/31 cages formed in vitro under high salt conditions in the absence of membrane (Stagg et al., 2006, 2008; Bhattacharya et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stagg et al., 2006, 2008; Bhattacharya et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2012.

claim: Comparison of vertices and edges in cages of different sizes (60–100 nm) has suggested geometrical rules governing outer coat assembly.
source: A comparison of the vertices and edges in cages of different sizes (60–100 nm) has suggested geometrical rules governing outer coat assembly, and indicated regions of flexibility in Sec13/31 that permit envelopment of vesicles with sizes ranging from 60 to 120 nm (Fath et al., 2007; Stagg et al., 2008; Bhattacharya et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fath et al., 2007; Stagg et al., 2008; Bhattacharya et al., 2012.

claim: Regions of flexibility in Sec13/31 permit envelopment of vesicles with sizes ranging from 60 to 120 nm.
source: A comparison of the vertices and edges in cages of different sizes (60–100 nm) has suggested geometrical rules governing outer coat assembly, and indicated regions of flexibility in Sec13/31 that permit envelopment of vesicles with sizes ranging from 60 to 120 nm (Fath et al., 2007; Stagg et al., 2008; Bhattacharya et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fath et al., 2007; Stagg et al., 2008; Bhattacharya et al., 2012.

claim: A higher degree of flexibility in COPII architecture is needed to explain the ability of COPII to mediate secretion of 300 nm pro-collagen fibres.
source: Nevertheless, a higher degree of flexibility in COPII architecture is needed to explain the ability of COPII to mediate secretion of cargoes such as 300 nm pro-collagen fibres, which are much larger than the 60–100 nm in vitro assembled cages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size discrepancy between known cage sizes and pro-collagen dimensions.

claim: Pro-collagen fibres are 300 nm in size.
source: Nevertheless, a higher degree of flexibility in COPII architecture is needed to explain the ability of COPII to mediate secretion of cargoes such as 300 nm pro-collagen fibres, which are much larger than the 60–100 nm in vitro assembled cages.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the size of pro-collagen fibres, representing established knowledge.

claim: Incorporation of pro-collagen into COPII coated vesicles is a highly regulated process.
source: There is increasing evidence that incorporation of pro-collagen into COPII coated vesicles is a highly regulated process, and that modifications in the outer coat proteins—such as ubiquitination—as well as in timing of GTP hydrolysis and coat recycling may be necessary for COPII ability to coat large vesicles (Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012.

claim: Modifications in the outer coat proteins such as ubiquitination may be necessary for COPII ability to coat large vesicles.
source: There is increasing evidence that incorporation of pro-collagen into COPII coated vesicles is a highly regulated process, and that modifications in the outer coat proteins—such as ubiquitination—as well as in timing of GTP hydrolysis and coat recycling may be necessary for COPII ability to coat large vesicles (Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012.

claim: Timing of GTP hydrolysis and coat recycling may be necessary for COPII ability to coat large vesicles.
source: There is increasing evidence that incorporation of pro-collagen into COPII coated vesicles is a highly regulated process, and that modifications in the outer coat proteins—such as ubiquitination—as well as in timing of GTP hydrolysis and coat recycling may be necessary for COPII ability to coat large vesicles (Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012.

claim: COPII-dependent defects in collagen transport are linked to Cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia.
source: COPII-dependent defects in collagen transport are linked to a genetic syndrome characterized by late-closing fontanels, sutural cataracts, facial dysmorphisms and skeletal defects: Cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (Boyadjiev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boyadjiev et al., 2006.

claim: Cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia is characterized by late-closing fontanels, sutural cataracts, facial dysmorphisms and skeletal defects.
source: COPII-dependent defects in collagen transport are linked to a genetic syndrome characterized by late-closing fontanels, sutural cataracts, facial dysmorphisms and skeletal defects: Cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (Boyadjiev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boyadjiev et al., 2006.

claim: There are currently no structural data on the COPII coat assembled in its functional state on a membrane.
source: There are currently no structural data on the COPII coat assembled in its functional state on a membrane, leaving important mechanistic questions unanswered.
evidence: This represents a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The authors incubated giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) with yeast COPII proteins in the presence of GMP-PNP.
source: We incubated giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) with yeast COPII proteins (Sec12, Sar1, Sec23/24, Sec13/31) in the presence of a non-hydrolysable GTP analogue GMP-PNP.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The authors imaged the reaction mixture by cryo-electron tomography.
source: We imaged the reaction mixture by cryo-electron tomography, observing that coated membranes of a variety of shapes and sizes were generated.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Coated membranes of a variety of shapes and sizes were generated in the reconstitution reaction.
source: We imaged the reaction mixture by cryo-electron tomography, observing that coated membranes of a variety of shapes and sizes were generated.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The coated membranes included round vesicles, either independent or still attached to the donor membrane, as well as curved or extended tubes.
source: These included round vesicles, either independent or still attached to the donor membrane, as well as curved or extended tubes, reminiscent of those detected budding from ER exit sites in vivo (Mironov et al., 2003; Fromme et al., 2007; Venditti et al., 2012; Figure 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1, with comparison to in vivo structures cited from literature.

claim: The observed tubular structures are reminiscent of those detected budding from ER exit sites in vivo.
source: These included round vesicles, either independent or still attached to the donor membrane, as well as curved or extended tubes, reminiscent of those detected budding from ER exit sites in vivo (Mironov et al., 2003; Fromme et al., 2007; Venditti et al., 2012; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison to in vivo structures supported by citations to Mironov et al., 2003; Fromme et al., 2007; Venditti et al., 2012.

claim: All of the coated structures were surrounded by two protein layers.
source: All of these structures were surrounded by two protein layers indicating that the COPII coat can assemble on membranes with a range of different curvatures.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The COPII coat can assemble on membranes with a range of different curvatures.
source: All of these structures were surrounded by two protein layers indicating that the COPII coat can assemble on membranes with a range of different curvatures.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that coated structures of various shapes were formed.

claim: The outer coat appeared in grazing slices as a regular arrangement of X-shaped features arrayed to form a rhomboidal lattice.
source: The outer coat appeared in sections as points or lines (Figure 1A), and in grazing slices as a regular arrangement of X-shaped features arrayed to form a rhomboidal lattice (a lozenge pattern) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Other geometries, such as triangles and pentagons, were observed on vesicles and tube ends.
source: Other geometries, such as triangles and pentagons, were observed on vesicles and tube ends (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The geometries observed on vesicles and tube ends are similar to those formed when purified Sec13/31 proteins assemble in vitro in the absence of a membrane.
source: These geometries are similar to those formed when purified Sec13/31 proteins assemble in vitro in the absence of a membrane (Stagg et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published structures, supported by citations to Stagg et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: The inner coat layer appeared as a regular array.
source: The inner coat layer also appeared as a regular array (Figure 1B), implying that Sar1 and Sec23/24 can also assemble to form a lattice.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sar1 and Sec23/24 can assemble to form a lattice.
source: The inner coat layer also appeared as a regular array (Figure 1B), implying that Sar1 and Sec23/24 can also assemble to form a lattice.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of regular arrays in the inner coat layer.

claim: The authors applied reference free, CTF corrected, subtomogram averaging to solve the 3D structure of the outer coat vertex to a resolution of approximately 40 Å.
source: To understand the architecture of the Sec13/31 outer coat we applied reference free, contrast-transfer function (CTF) corrected, subtomogram averaging to solve the 3D structure of the vertex, and of the connecting rods to resolutions of ∼40 Å (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and resolution achieved, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The authors solved the 3D structure of the connecting rods to a resolution of approximately 40 Å.
source: To understand the architecture of the Sec13/31 outer coat we applied reference free, contrast-transfer function (CTF) corrected, subtomogram averaging to solve the 3D structure of the vertex, and of the connecting rods to resolutions of ∼40 Å (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and resolution achieved, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The vertex structure was a twofold symmetric X-shape, similar to that seen in in vitro assembled Sec13/31 cages.
source: The vertex structure was a twofold symmetric X-shape, similar to that seen in in vitro assembled Sec13/31 cages (Stagg et al., 2006, 2008) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data, compared to previously published structures cited from Stagg et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: The connecting rods are consistent in shape and size with Sec13/31 heterotetramers.
source: The connecting rods are consistent in shape and size with Sec13/31 heterotetramers, and are bent in the middle by approximately 15°.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data.

claim: The connecting rods are bent in the middle by approximately 15°.
source: The connecting rods are consistent in shape and size with Sec13/31 heterotetramers, and are bent in the middle by approximately 15°.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data.

claim: The 15° bend in the rods is seen in the solved X-ray crystal structure.
source: This same bend is seen in the solved X-ray crystal structure, which can be fitted into the densities as a rigid body (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a comparison to the X-ray crystal structure, shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The X-ray crystal structure can be fitted into the densities as a rigid body.
source: This same bend is seen in the solved X-ray crystal structure, which can be fitted into the densities as a rigid body (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This describes the fitting of atomic models into the EM density, shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: There is a 45° bend in the rods of in vitro-assembled protein cages.
source: In contrast, there is a 45° bend in the rods of in vitro-assembled protein cages (Stagg et al., 2008; Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published structures, supported by citation to Stagg et al., 2008 and shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The central hinge between Sec31 molecules can adapt to assemble coats of different curvatures.
source: These data indicate that the central hinge between Sec31 molecules can adapt to assemble coats of different curvatures.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of different bend angles in different contexts.

claim: The authors applied reference-free, CTF corrected, subtomogram averaging to solve the structure of the repeating inner coat unit with a resolution of approximately 23 Å.
source: We applied reference-free, CTF corrected, subtomogram averaging to solve the structure of the repeating inner coat unit with a resolution of approximately 23 Å (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; 'Materials and methods' and Faini et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and resolution achieved, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The bow-tie-shaped repeating unit interacts tightly with the outer membrane leaflet.
source: The bow-tie-shaped repeating unit interacts tightly with the outer membrane leaflet.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data.

claim: The inner coat units interact with each other to form an approximately helical array on the tube surface.
source: The units interact with each other to form an approximately helical array on the tube surface (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Step changes in tube diameter are associated with displacement of a few subunits from the lattice.
source: In many instances we see step changes in tube diameter, associated with displacement of a few subunits from the lattice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The crystal structures of Sec23/Sar1 and Sec23/24 fit unambiguously into one bow-tie shaped subunit as rigid bodies.
source: We docked the crystal structures of Sec23/Sar1 (PDB 2QTV), and of Sec23/24 (PDB 1M2V) (Bi et al., 2002) into the subtomogram averaging electron density map. Both fit unambiguously into one bow-tie shaped subunit as rigid bodies, in each case placing Sec23 in the same position ('Materials and methods'; Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the fitting of atomic models into the EM density, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both Sec23/Sar1 and Sec23/24 structures place Sec23 in the same position when fitted into the density.
source: We docked the crystal structures of Sec23/Sar1 (PDB 2QTV), and of Sec23/24 (PDB 1M2V) (Bi et al., 2002) into the subtomogram averaging electron density map. Both fit unambiguously into one bow-tie shaped subunit as rigid bodies, in each case placing Sec23 in the same position ('Materials and methods'; Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the fitting of atomic models into the EM density, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Two interfaces between the long edges of the Sar1/Sec23/24 heterotrimer mediate formation of lattice rows.
source: Analysis of the fitted models reveals the novel network of interactions that mediate lattice formation and membrane binding. Two interfaces between the long edges of the Sar1/Sec23/24 heterotrimer mediate formation of lattice rows.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models.

claim: The larger interface involves Sar1, the gelsolin-like and the C-terminal domain of Sec23 from one heterotrimer interacting with the Zn-finger and part of the beta barrel domains of Sec23 in the adjacent heterotrimer.
source: The larger involves Sar1, the gelsolin-like and the C-terminal domain of Sec23 from one heterotrimer interacting with the Zn-finger and part of the beta barrel domains of Sec23 in the adjacent heterotrimer.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models.

claim: The smaller interface is between the Zn-finger domain of Sec24 in one heterotrimer and the gelsolin-like and C-terminal domains of Sec24 in the neighbouring heterotrimer.
source: The smaller interface is between the Zn-finger domain of Sec24 in one heterotrimer and the gelsolin-like and C-terminal domains of Sec24 in the neighbouring heterotrimer (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The contacts between heterotrimers are characterised by extended surfaces with opposite charges.
source: These contacts are characterised by extended surfaces with opposite charges, a property that is conserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The property of opposite charges at the interfaces is conserved.
source: These contacts are characterised by extended surfaces with opposite charges, a property that is conserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models across species, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rows contact each other where the beta barrel domain of Sec23 approaches the Sec24 N-terminus.
source: The rows contact each other where the beta barrel domain of Sec23 approaches the Sec24 N-terminus.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models.

claim: In the Sec23/24 crystal structure, the Sec24 N-terminal helix 61-73 forms a crystallographic contact with the beta-barrel domain of Sec23 in the neighbouring asymmetric unit.
source: In the Sec23/24 crystal structure (PDB ID 1M2V), the Sec24 N-terminal helix 61-73 forms a crystallographic contact with the beta-barrel domain of Sec23 in the neighbouring asymmetric unit (Bi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the crystal structure, supported by citation to Bi et al., 2002.

claim: When placed in the position from the crystal structure, the 61–73 helix fills an unoccupied region of electron density in the assembled coat structure.
source: When placed in this position, the 61–73 helix fills an unoccupied region of electron density in our structure, suggesting this contact is present in the assembled coat (Figure 5A,B, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the atomic model into the EM density, shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The contact between the Sec24 61-73 helix and Sec23 beta-barrel is present in the assembled coat.
source: When placed in this position, the 61–73 helix fills an unoccupied region of electron density in our structure, suggesting this contact is present in the assembled coat (Figure 5A,B, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an inference from the fitting of the atomic model into the EM density.

claim: The concave surface of the inner coat heterotrimer is oriented towards the membrane.
source: Our structure reveals that the concave surface of the inner coat heterotrimer is oriented towards the membrane and the Sec31 binding site towards the coat exterior (Figure 5A,C), as previously predicted (Bi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data shown in Figure 5A,C, consistent with previous predictions cited from Bi et al., 2002.

claim: The Sec31 binding site is oriented towards the coat exterior.
source: Our structure reveals that the concave surface of the inner coat heterotrimer is oriented towards the membrane and the Sec31 binding site towards the coat exterior (Figure 5A,C), as previously predicted (Bi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data shown in Figure 5A,C, consistent with previous predictions cited from Bi et al., 2002.

claim: One membrane interacting region is formed by a small part of Sec23 together with Sar1, orienting Sar1 to direct its N-terminal amphipathic helix into the outer leaflet.
source: We identify two primary membrane interacting regions. One is formed by a small part of Sec23 together with Sar1, orienting Sar1 to direct its N-terminal amphipathic helix into the outer leaflet.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models.

claim: The other membrane interacting region is a large basic surface in Sec24, including the Sec24 Zn finger, beta barrel and alpha helical domains.
source: The other is a large basic surface in Sec24, including the Sec24 Zn finger, beta barrel and alpha helical domains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Sec24 Zn finger domain binds the membrane.
source: While the Sec24 Zn finger domain binds the membrane, the Sec23 Zn finger domain does not, instead it faces the neighbouring heterotrimer, suggesting that the role of the Zn fingers in Sec23 and Sec24 has diverged.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models.

claim: The Sec23 Zn finger domain does not bind the membrane but faces the neighbouring heterotrimer.
source: While the Sec24 Zn finger domain binds the membrane, the Sec23 Zn finger domain does not, instead it faces the neighbouring heterotrimer, suggesting that the role of the Zn fingers in Sec23 and Sec24 has diverged.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models.

claim: The role of the Zn fingers in Sec23 and Sec24 has diverged.
source: While the Sec24 Zn finger domain binds the membrane, the Sec23 Zn finger domain does not, instead it faces the neighbouring heterotrimer, suggesting that the role of the Zn fingers in Sec23 and Sec24 has diverged.
evidence: This is an inference from the different orientations and functions of the Zn fingers.

claim: The Sec24 Zn finger is essential for cell survival.
source: Consistent with this difference in function, the Sec24 Zn finger, essential for cell survival (Peng et al., 1999), contains a conserved basic patch that is absent in Sec23.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 1999.

claim: The Sec24 Zn finger contains a conserved basic patch that is absent in Sec23.
source: Consistent with this difference in function, the Sec24 Zn finger, essential for cell survival (Peng et al., 1999), contains a conserved basic patch that is absent in Sec23.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models and sequence conservation.

claim: The conserved basic patch in the Sec24 Zn finger represents a phospholipid-binding site, analogous to the basic Zn fingers in FYVE domains.
source: We speculate that, analogous to the basic Zn fingers in FYVE domains (Gaullier et al., 2000), this represents a phospholipid-binding site.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to FYVE domains, supported by citation to Gaullier et al., 2000.

claim: The trunk domains of Sec23 and Sec24 do not contact the membrane but are suspended above it.
source: The trunk domains of Sec23 and Sec24 do not contact the membrane but are suspended above it, leaving space that would allow binding to more highly curved vesicles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The space between trunk domains and membrane would allow binding to more highly curved vesicles.
source: The trunk domains of Sec23 and Sec24 do not contact the membrane but are suspended above it, leaving space that would allow binding to more highly curved vesicles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural arrangement.

claim: None of the characterised cargo-binding sites overlap with the protein–protein and protein–membrane interfaces identified in the lattice.
source: To test this, we modelled the X-ray structures of Sec24 co-crystallised with cargo-derived peptides (Mossessova et al., 2003; Mancias and Goldberg, 2007, 2008), or the cytosolic domain of a globular cargo Sec22 (Mancias and Goldberg, 2007) in our map. None of the characterised cargo-binding sites overlap with the protein–protein and protein–membrane interfaces we identified in the lattice: all remain accessible to cargo in the assembled inner coat (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from modeling cargo-binding structures into the EM density, shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: All cargo-binding sites remain accessible to cargo in the assembled inner coat.
source: To test this, we modelled the X-ray structures of Sec24 co-crystallised with cargo-derived peptides (Mossessova et al., 2003; Mancias and Goldberg, 2007, 2008), or the cytosolic domain of a globular cargo Sec22 (Mancias and Goldberg, 2007) in our map. None of the characterised cargo-binding sites overlap with the protein–protein and protein–membrane interfaces we identified in the lattice: all remain accessible to cargo in the assembled inner coat (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from modeling cargo-binding structures into the EM density, shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The space between heterotrimers in the assembled inner coat lattice forms a pocket into which Sec22 would bind.
source: Strikingly, comparison of the co-crystal structure of Sec23/24/Sec22 with our density map reveals that the space between heterotrimers in the assembled inner coat lattice forms a pocket into which Sec22 would bind (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from modeling the Sec22 co-crystal structure into the EM density, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The interfaces between heterotrimers have conserved electrostatic properties.
source: Three factors suggest, however, that the interactions we observe between heterotrimers are relevant in vivo and are not simply an artefact of in vitro assembly. Firstly, they result from a productive assembly reaction that bends the GUV membrane into a variety of shapes. Secondly, the interfaces have conserved electrostatic properties.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models across species.

claim: The interactions between heterotrimers result from a productive assembly reaction that bends the GUV membrane into a variety of shapes.
source: Three factors suggest, however, that the interactions we observe between heterotrimers are relevant in vivo and are not simply an artefact of in vitro assembly. Firstly, they result from a productive assembly reaction that bends the GUV membrane into a variety of shapes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The interactions that mediate inner coat lattice assembly are distinct from those that mediate membrane binding, outer coat binding, and cargo binding.
source: Thirdly, the interactions that mediate inner coat lattice assembly are distinct from those that mediate membrane binding, outer coat binding, and cargo binding and can accommodate Sec22 in the correct position: they are fully compatible with available biochemical and structural data.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the fitted atomic models and comparison to known binding sites.

claim: The interactions that mediate inner coat lattice assembly can accommodate Sec22 in the correct position.
source: Thirdly, the interactions that mediate inner coat lattice assembly are distinct from those that mediate membrane binding, outer coat binding, and cargo binding and can accommodate Sec22 in the correct position: they are fully compatible with available biochemical and structural data.
evidence: This is a finding from modeling the Sec22 co-crystal structure into the EM density.

claim: The structure of the outer coat does not reveal density corresponding to an ordered inner coat.
source: Our structure of the outer coat does not reveal density corresponding to an ordered inner coat, and vice versa, indicating that the relative positions of the two coat layers are not fixed.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data.

claim: The structure of the inner coat does not reveal density corresponding to an ordered outer coat.
source: Our structure of the outer coat does not reveal density corresponding to an ordered inner coat, and vice versa, indicating that the relative positions of the two coat layers are not fixed.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data.

claim: The relative positions of the two coat layers are not fixed.
source: Our structure of the outer coat does not reveal density corresponding to an ordered inner coat, and vice versa, indicating that the relative positions of the two coat layers are not fixed.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that each coat structure does not show ordered density for the other coat.

claim: The two coat layers are approximately aligned both in spacing and orientation.
source: Nevertheless, the two layers are approximately aligned both in spacing and orientation.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the positions of aligned structures.

claim: The 'rows' in the inner coat are aligned to the left-handed rods of the outer coat, with four inner coat heterotrimers spanning one outer coat rod.
source: The 'rows' in the inner coat are aligned to the left-handed rods of the outer coat, with four inner coat heterotrimers spanning one outer coat rod.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the positions of aligned structures.

claim: The inner coat 'columns' are aligned to the right-handed outer coat rods, with two inner coat heterotrimers spanning one outer coat rod.
source: The inner coat 'columns' are aligned to the right-handed outer coat rods, with two inner coat heterotrimers spanning one outer coat rod (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the positions of aligned structures, shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The unstructured C-terminal region of Sec31 connects the inner and outer coats.
source: This relationship suggests that the unstructured C-terminal region of Sec31 (Fath et al., 2007; Noble et al., 2012), which connects the inner and outer coats, constrains the coat layers but does not fix their absolute positions, much like multiple anchor cables on a ship.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fath et al., 2007 and Noble et al., 2012.

claim: The unstructured C-terminal region of Sec31 constrains the coat layers but does not fix their absolute positions.
source: This relationship suggests that the unstructured C-terminal region of Sec31 (Fath et al., 2007; Noble et al., 2012), which connects the inner and outer coats, constrains the coat layers but does not fix their absolute positions, much like multiple anchor cables on a ship.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of approximate but not fixed alignment of the two coat layers.

claim: Flexibility in the relative positions of the two layers would permit adaptation of the coat to variable curvatures.
source: This flexibility in the relative positions of the two layers would permit adaptation of the coat to variable curvatures.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings.

claim: Gaps and dislocations in both inner and outer coat lattices may contribute to curvature variability.
source: Gaps and dislocations in both inner and outer coat lattices may further contribute to curvature variability.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations of lattice irregularities.

claim: The spherical tube ends have an outer coat arrangement similar to that previously observed in in vitro cages.
source: The spherical tube ends have an outer coat arrangement similar to that previously observed in in vitro cages, in which adjacent vertices are rotated relative to one another.
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published structures.

claim: A helical array of the inner coat heterotrimer cannot be present on the spherically-curved tips.
source: A helical array of the inner coat heterotrimer cannot be present on the spherically-curved tips.
evidence: This is an inference based on geometric constraints.

claim: On the tube tips, the inner coat lattice is likely arranged in smaller patches rotated relative to one another, each maintaining the same relationship to the overlying outer coat vertex.
source: Instead, we consider it likely that on the tube tips, the inner coat lattice is arranged in smaller patches rotated relative to one another, each maintaining the same relationship to the overlying outer coat vertex.
evidence: This is speculation based on geometric constraints and the observed relationship between inner and outer coats.

claim: Gaps between or within lattice patches could accommodate cargoes with large membrane-proximal domains.
source: Gaps between or within lattice patches could accommodate cargoes with large membrane-proximal domains.
evidence: This is speculation about how the structure could accommodate large cargoes.

claim: Both inner and outer COPII layers have sufficient structural versatility to coat both spherical and tubular membranes.
source: The structural data we have presented shows that both inner and outer COPII layers have sufficient structural versatility to coat both spherical and tubular membranes, and thereby accommodate important large cargoes such as pro-collagen.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural data showing coats on different membrane geometries.

claim: Both coats can assemble regular lattices with constrained relative positions.
source: We found that both coats can assemble regular lattices with constrained relative positions.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural data.

claim: The relationship between inner and outer coats would permit the inner coat to influence the arrangement of the outer coat.
source: This relationship would permit the inner coat to influence the arrangement of the outer coat and therefore to play a critical structural role in determining vesicle shape.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed constrained relationship between the two coats.

claim: The inner coat could play a critical structural role in determining vesicle shape.
source: This relationship would permit the inner coat to influence the arrangement of the outer coat and therefore to play a critical structural role in determining vesicle shape.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed constrained relationship between the two coats.

claim: The formation of larger arrays of the inner coat and associated rhomboidal outer coat lattices could favour the formation of larger tubular carriers able to accommodate cargoes such as pro-collagen.
source: Our data hint at the possibility that the formation of larger arrays of the inner coat and the formation of associated rhomboidal outer coat lattices, could favour the formation of larger tubular carriers able to accommodate cargoes such as pro-collagen.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural findings.

claim: TANGO1 and Sedlin act in concert to stabilize the inner coat, modulating Sar1 GTPase activity and delaying both outer coat recruitment and scission.
source: It has previously been proposed that proteins such as TANGO1 and Sedlin (Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012) act in concert to stabilize the inner coat, modulating Sar1 GTPase activity and delaying both outer coat recruitment and scission.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Venditti et al., 2012.

claim: Stabilization of the inner coat could promote growth of larger carriers not only by delaying scission, but also by promoting tubular membrane morphology.
source: We suggest that stabilization of the inner coat could promote growth of larger carriers not only by delaying scission, but also by promoting tubular membrane morphology (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In the tubular membranes, the rods oriented in one direction (right handed rods) each make two '+' contacts.
source: In this arrangement of vertices the rods oriented in one direction (the right handed rods, purple in Figures 2C and 3B) each make two '+' contacts (+/+), while the left-handed rods (green in Figures 2C and 3B) each make two '−' contacts (−/−).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the vertex and rod structures on tubular membranes, shown in Figures 2C and 3B.

claim: In the tubular membranes, the left-handed rods each make two '−' contacts.
source: In this arrangement of vertices the rods oriented in one direction (the right handed rods, purple in Figures 2C and 3B) each make two '+' contacts (+/+), while the left-handed rods (green in Figures 2C and 3B) each make two '−' contacts (−/−).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the vertex and rod structures on tubular membranes, shown in Figures 2C and 3B.

claim: The alpha angle on tubular membranes is 79.7° ± 5.9° and is oriented around the tube circumference.
source: The alpha angle is 79.7° ± 5.9° and is oriented around the tube circumference while the beta angle is 95.7° ± 5.8° and is oriented along the tube axis (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data, shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The beta angle on tubular membranes is 95.7° ± 5.8° and is oriented along the tube axis.
source: The alpha angle is 79.7° ± 5.9° and is oriented around the tube circumference while the beta angle is 95.7° ± 5.8° and is oriented along the tube axis (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data, shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Three properties contribute to outer coat adaptability: variability of both alpha and beta angles at the vertices, flexibility of the central rod hinge, and the absence of any inherent asymmetry in the Sec13/31 rods.
source: Together these data imply that three properties contribute to outer coat adaptability: (i) variability of both alpha and beta angles at the vertices, (ii) flexibility of the central rod hinge, and (iii) the absence of any inherent asymmetry in the Sec13/31 rods, allowing them to make '+' contacts at both ends, '−' contacts at both ends, or a '+' contact at one end and a '−' contact at the other.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings.

claim: The absence of inherent asymmetry in Sec13/31 rods allows them to make '+' contacts at both ends, '−' contacts at both ends, or a '+' contact at one end and a '−' contact at the other.
source: Together these data imply that three properties contribute to outer coat adaptability: (i) variability of both alpha and beta angles at the vertices, (ii) flexibility of the central rod hinge, and (iii) the absence of any inherent asymmetry in the Sec13/31 rods, allowing them to make '+' contacts at both ends, '−' contacts at both ends, or a '+' contact at one end and a '−' contact at the other.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings.

claim: The versatility of the outer coat allows coating of not only spherical, but also tubular membranes.
source: Together this versatility allows coating of not only spherical, but also of tubular membranes and therefore accommodation of large elongated cargoes such as pro-collagen.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings showing coats on different membrane geometries.

claim: The versatility of the outer coat allows accommodation of large elongated cargoes such as pro-collagen.
source: Together this versatility allows coating of not only spherical, but also of tubular membranes and therefore accommodation of large elongated cargoes such as pro-collagen.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural findings showing coats on tubular membranes.

claim: Flexibility in outer coat cage geometry is primarily mediated by subtly varying contacts at multiple hinge positions in the rod and vertex.
source: It seems likely that flexibility in the outer COPII cage geometry is primarily mediated by subtly varying contacts at multiple hinge positions in the rod and vertex (Noble et al., 2012), but we cannot rule out the presence of structural switches.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural findings and comparison to other systems, with citation to Noble et al., 2012.

claim: The presence of structural switches in the outer coat cannot be ruled out.
source: It seems likely that flexibility in the outer COPII cage geometry is primarily mediated by subtly varying contacts at multiple hinge positions in the rod and vertex (Noble et al., 2012), but we cannot rule out the presence of structural switches.
evidence: This acknowledges an alternative possibility that cannot be excluded.

claim: The inner coat may not only function to link cargo and membrane to the outer coat, but also play a structural role in determining vesicle shape.
source: Our images showed that the inner coat can also form a regular lattice, suggesting it may not only function to link cargo and membrane to the outer coat, but also play a structural role in determining vesicle shape.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of regular inner coat lattices.

claim: The unit cell angles for the inner coat lattice are 83.8° ± 10° and 95.4° ± 9.8°.
source: The unit cell angles for the inner coat lattice are 83.8° ± 10° and 95.4° ± 9.8°, very close to the angles of 79.7° ± 5.9° (alpha) and 95.7° ± 5.8° (beta) measured for the outer coat.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The distance between neighbouring outer coat vertices in the right-handed direction (30.2 ± 2 nm) is similar to the distance between two rows of inner coat subunits (30.2 ± 2 nm).
source: The distance between neighbouring outer coat vertices in the right-handed direction (30.2 ± 2 nm) is similar to the distance between two rows of inner coat subunits (30.2 ± 2 nm), while the distance between outer coat vertices in the left-handed direction (31.9 ± 1.9 nm) is similar to the distance between 4 inner coat subunits (31.4 ± 4.5 nm).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The distance between outer coat vertices in the left-handed direction (31.9 ± 1.9 nm) is similar to the distance between 4 inner coat subunits (31.4 ± 4.5 nm).
source: The distance between neighbouring outer coat vertices in the right-handed direction (30.2 ± 2 nm) is similar to the distance between two rows of inner coat subunits (30.2 ± 2 nm), while the distance between outer coat vertices in the left-handed direction (31.9 ± 1.9 nm) is similar to the distance between 4 inner coat subunits (31.4 ± 4.5 nm).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The two lattices (inner and outer coat) are very closely matched.
source: The two lattices are therefore very closely matched.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the measurements showing similar angles and distances.
